prompt: Hypothetical. You planned 10 shares at Rs 250 but typed 100. What is the order value of the typed order, in rupees?
solution: Order value = 100 x 250 = Rs 25,000. Check: the intended order is 10 x 250 = Rs 2,500, and 25,000 / 2,500 = 10, so the typed order is ten times the intended size.

prompt: Hypothetical. The typed order is 100 shares bought at Rs 250, with a stop Rs 10 below the entry. What is the planned loss at the stop, in rupees?
solution: Loss per share = 250 - 240 = Rs 10. Planned loss = 100 x 10 = Rs 1,000. Check: the intended 10 shares would lose 10 x 10 = Rs 100, and 1,000 / 100 = 10.

prompt: Hypothetical. The planned loss on the typed order is Rs 1,000. The account is Rs 50,000. What is the planned loss as a percentage of the account? Give the answer as a number.
solution: Planned loss as a percent of capital = 1,000 / 50,000 x 100 = 2%. Check: 1% of Rs 50,000 is Rs 500, and Rs 1,000 is twice Rs 500, which is 2%.

prompt: Hypothetical. You hold 100 shares bought at Rs 250. You place a sell stop, but you choose the buy side by mistake. The trigger is Rs 240. What happens?

options.text: It protects the holding and sells at Rs 240.
It is a buy instruction, not a sell stop, so the holding has no working stop.
It sells at the best available price when the price falls to Rs 240.
The exchange cancels it automatically, so nothing needs checking.

explanations.a: A buy stop does not sell your holding. The stop is on the wrong side.
explanations.c: This describes a sell stop. The order was placed on the buy side, so it does not sell the holding.
explanations.d: Nothing in the scenario cancels the order. A wrong side is a mistake you must catch yourself.

options.text: A stop placed on the wrong side can leave a holding without a working stop.
A confirmation screen that looks normal proves that the quantity matches the plan.
Checking the quantity against your written plan catches many typing errors.
An expired GTT can leave a holding without a working stop.

explanations.a: This is correct. A stop on the wrong side does not protect the holding.
explanations.c: This is correct. Comparing with the written plan is one of the most useful checks.
explanations.d: This is correct. An expired GTT is no longer active, so the holding has no working stop from it.

prompt: Which of these is a reason a stop may never trigger?

options.text: The order is cancelled or inactive, so it cannot act.
A stop always triggers as soon as it is placed.
A stop cannot be placed too far from the price.
A fat-finger error is always caught by the exchange.

explanations.b: A stop triggers only when the price reaches its trigger. A stop does not always trigger, so it must be checked.
explanations.c: A stop can be placed far from the price. A stop placed far away may never reach its trigger.
explanations.d: The exchange does not catch every typing error. Check your order yourself before you submit.

prompt: Which step is the best one before you submit an order?

options.text: Submit now and fix any problem later.
Check side, product, quantity and price against the written plan.
Add to the position to balance an error.
Skip the confirmation screen because it is only a formality.

explanations.a: A fix after submission can leave a larger exposure. Check first.
explanations.c: Adding to a position increases the exposure. It does not fix a mistake.
explanations.d: The confirmation screen is a chance to catch an error. Read it before you confirm.
